title: June 1984, remembered again
hookLine: in Sikh remembrance, the June 1984 attack is the third ghallughara

lines: AN OLD WORD, A NEW NUMBER.
cards: Some words are names for a single thing. Others are names for a kind of thing, so that when something new happens, people reach for the old word and add a number. Sikhs have such a word.
It belongs to the long story this year has been walking: two great massacres of Sikhs, long ago, remembered as the small and the great ghallughara.
When the army entered the Darbar Sahib in the June this lesson is named for, a new event got the old word. In Sikh remembrance it is the third ghallughara.

teach.b: First, the word. Ghallughara means a holocaust, a massacre, a great destruction. This path met the small and the great ghallughara earlier this year, in the years when Sikhs were hunted and killed.
Second, the June. The government called it Operation Blue Star. Bhindranwale and armed followers had fortified the Darbar Sahib complex, and the army was sent in to remove them.
It came during the days Sikhs gather to remember the martyrdom of Guru Arjan, the Guru who compiled the Adi Granth, so the complex was full of pilgrims. Pilgrims died alongside fighters and soldiers.
The Akal Takht was badly damaged in the fighting. The Sikh Reference Library, with its old handwritten books, burned. Third, the naming.

teach.h: A LINE WITH THE EARLIER TWO.
teach.b: Calling June the third ghallughara puts it in a line with the two earlier massacres. It says this belongs to the Sikh story of suffering, and is remembered the same way: in gatherings and in prayer, every June.
Others, including the government of the day, described it as a military operation against armed militants. Both descriptions are part of the record. Fourth, the root.
Guru Arjan, whose martyrdom the pilgrims had come to mark, wrote at Ang 394 that whatever the Lord does seems sweet to him.
Sikhs remember that line beside his martyrdom. Holding it in June is not saying that what happened was sweet. It is how a tradition grieves without letting go of its Guru.

how: Sikhs remember the June attack on the Darbar Sahib each year, with gatherings at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras, where those who died are remembered in prayer.

o: a battle the Khalsa won against long odds
a great destruction, a massacre remembered in prayer
a festival held each June at the Golden Temple

games.q: an old word, a new number — tap the pairs.
p: Guru Arjan: your will seems sweet

s: the complex was nearly empty when the army came
it came during the days of Guru Arjan's martyrdom remembrance, and pilgrims were inside.
its old handwritten books were lost in the fire.
everyone describes June in the same words
Sikh remembrance calls it the third ghallughara; the government described a military operation against armed militants.

games.q: you're naming a terrible event so it is never forgotten. what do you reach for?
o: a brand-new name, so it stands alone.
an old word with a number, so it joins a line.
games.why: Sikh memory reached for the old word and added a number: the third ghallughara, in a line with the small and the great.

practice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp; if not, picture one, and look at the flame.

The pilgrims came that June to remember a Guru's martyrdom, and some never went home, so breathe in and let the light stand for them, the old and the young, without names, and breathe out holding their families.
If you pray, say Waheguru, and let the flame burn.

wordCard.voice: Ghallughara. A great destruction, a massacre. Sikh memory holds two from the long story, and calls the June attack on the Darbar Sahib the third. Today's word.

orig.note: a great destruction or massacre; the word for the two earlier ones, and for June.

carryVoice: Your line: the third ghallughara. Grief, held without letting go of the Guru. Gently, see you tomorrow.
